pages.page_summary: Nick sits at his desk at night, opens a notebook, and begins writing his account; as he writes, he recalls his father's advice, considers how reserving judgment has shaped his life, and admits that his tolerance has a limit—he has come back from the East wanting the world at moral attention.

panels.beat: Nick, alone at a lamp-lit desk at night, opens a notebook and uncaps his pen; behind him a window shows the dim Midwestern dusk. He pauses to remember his father's long-ago advice.

pages.page_summary: At his desk, Nick writes about the one exception to his scorn—Gatsby—then turns the page to his own history: graduating, returning restless from the Great War, securing his father's backing, and arriving East in spring 1922 where a coworker's suggestion points him toward a commuter town.

panels.beat: Nick at his desk pauses over the notebook; in the ghosted window-reflection, a tall silhouette resolves—Gatsby, the one exception, sensed but unseen.

Warm desk-lamp light on Nick's hands and face; cool blue night beyond. Sepia and dusk-blue palette. panels.beat: Memory unfurls: a young Nick in uniform returns from the Great War to his prominent Midwestern family's parlor; the homecoming is warm but he is already restless, the Midwest now feeling like the ragged edge of the world.

His expression is polite but distant, restless. Edges of the panel feather into cream. panels.caption: My family have been prominent, well-to-do people in this Middle Western city for three generations. I graduated from New Haven in 1915, and later took part in that delayed Teutonic migration known as the Great War. // I enjoyed the counter-raid so thoroughly that I came back restless—the Middle West now seemed the ragged edge of the universe.
panels.continuity_notes: Memory frame: feathered edges, warmer wash, softer line, as established for remembered scenes.
panels.adaptation_note: Compresses biographical exposition into one staged homecoming so it reads as a single observable beat, not a montage.

panels.caption: So I decided to go East and learn the bond business. Father agreed to finance me for a year, and I came East, permanently, I thought, in the spring of twenty-two. // When a young man at the office suggested we take a house together in a commuting town, it sounded like a great idea.

pages.page_summary: Nick moves alone into the weather-beaten West Egg bungalow, settles into solitary routines with a Finnish cook, is asked directions by a newer arrival on the road (which converts his loneliness into a sense of belonging), and begins his summer of self-improvement by shelving a stack of finance volumes—setting up his arrival in one of the strangest communities in North America.

panels.beat: Back inside the bungalow study, Nick shelves a dozen red-and-gold finance volumes by a sunlit window, beginning his summer program of self-improvement.
panels.image_prompt: Interior medium shot of a small study in the bungalow. Nick Carraway in shirtsleeves, loosened tie, and suspenders stands at a low bookshelf beneath a window, sliding a thick red-and-gold-bound volume into place beside eleven matching volumes. On the desk beside him: a single lit desk lamp, an open notebook with pen, and a framed photograph of his father. Beyond the window, a hint of green lawn and a sliver of bright water in late spring sunlight. Warm lamplight blending with cool daylight from the window; soft sepia and dusk-blue watercolor wash. Reserve clean wall area above the bookshelf and a clear bottom band for two stacked caption boxes; no readable text, no lettering, no signage anywhere in the art. panels.caption: With the sunshine and the bursting leaves, I had that familiar conviction that life was beginning over again with the summer. I bought a dozen volumes on banking and credit—red and gold like new money from the mint—and meant once more to become the 'well-rounded man.' It was a matter of chance that I should have rented a house in one of the strangest communities in North America.
panels.continuity_notes: Desk lamp, notebook, and father's photograph carry forward from page 1. Sliver of water through the window foreshadows the West Egg/East Egg geography to be opened on page 4.
panels.adaptation_note: Single concrete action—shelving the finance books at the window—anchors five short reflective units; closing caption seeds the West Egg reveal.

pages.page_summary: Nick steps out of his bungalow onto the lawn and takes in his surroundings: he surveys the twin eggs of Long Island across the bay, then turns to find his small house dwarfed by Gatsby's colossal mansion next door. The abstract geography is anchored to his physical walk from doorstep to the property line, where he first lays eyes on the neighbor he does not yet know.

panels.beat: Nick steps out of his bungalow door onto the lawn, shading his eyes toward the Sound; the two eggs of Long Island are visible as low promontories across a glittering courtesy bay.

Middle distance: a domesticated salt-water bay separating two matching tongues of land jutting east, dotted with estate rooftops and trees. panels.caption: It was on that slender riotous island which extends itself due east of New York—where, twenty miles from the city, a pair of enormous eggs jut into the great wet barnyard of Long Island Sound.

panels.caption: My house, at the very tip of the egg, was squeezed between two huge places that rented for twelve or fifteen thousand a season. The one on my right was a colossal affair—a factual imitation of some Hôtel de Ville in Normandy, with a tower, a marble swimming pool, and more than forty acres of lawn and garden.
panels.continuity_notes: First concrete reveal of Gatsby's mansion next door, anchored to Nick's walk along the property line.

panels.caption: It was Gatsby's mansion. Or, rather, as I didn't know Mr. Gatsby, it was a mansion inhabited by a gentleman of that name. My own house was an eyesore, but a small eyesore—and it had been overlooked, so I had a view of the water, a partial view of my neighbour's lawn, and the consoling proximity of millionaires—all for eighty dollars a month.
panels.continuity_notes: Gatsby named for the first time; Nick remains physically anchored at his bungalow.
